transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hello. Well, I came in because... ever since the school district put this new bilingual social-emotional learning rollout on my plate, right on top of my regular teaching, I've just been feeling off. I mean, I still get through the day, but I feel so wound up and discouraged in a way that really isn't like me. I've even started putting off my lesson plans and avoiding emails that I used to just handle without a second thought.
When you say you feel 'wound up,' can you describe what that feels like physically or mentally—for example, are you experiencing racing thoughts, muscle tension, or something else?

Um, I haven't really noticed anything specific like muscle tension or... or my thoughts racing, exactly. I'm not really sure how to describe it physically. It's just more of a... a general feeling of being on edge all day, I guess. But no, I haven't really had any physical aches or anything like what you mentioned.
Since this new teaching assignment started, have you been feeling down, sad, or depressed most of the day?

Well, no, not really. I wouldn't say I feel sad or depressed most of the day. I mean, I feel a bit discouraged sometimes when I think about everything I have to get done, like I mentioned earlier, but... no, I don't really feel down like that. It's mostly just that on-edge feeling.
Since this new teaching assignment started, how long have you been feeling this on-edge feeling—is it pretty much every day, or does it come and go?
Well, it's pretty much every day now. It started about five months ago, right when the district assigned me this rollout role midyear. Ever since then, it's just been this constant, daily thing.
Besides feeling on edge, have you noticed other things like difficulty concentrating, sleep problems, irritability, or restlessness over these past five months?

No, not really. I mean, I'm sleeping fine, and I don't think I'm any more irritable than usual. My concentration is okay too, I'm still getting my work done. It's really just that on-edge feeling I mentioned.
When you're not thinking about the school district assignment or your teaching responsibilities, do you still feel that on-edge feeling, or does it mostly go away?

No, it mostly goes away. If I'm, say, relaxing on the weekend and managing to keep my mind off school, I feel fine. It really only flares up when I start thinking about the district rollout or all my teaching duties. When I'm not focused on that, I don't really feel on edge at all.

You mentioned the on-edge feeling goes away when you're not thinking about school—but are there other situations outside of school, like social gatherings, being around other people, or everyday activities, where you also feel that on-edge feeling?

No, not at all. If I'm at a social gathering or just out running errands and doing everyday things, I'm perfectly fine. I don't get that feeling when I'm around other people outside of work. It really is just entirely tied to the school situation.

When you think about the school district rollout and your teaching duties, what specifically worries you about it? Is it mainly the workload itself, or do you find yourself worrying about things like whether you'll be able to handle it, what might go wrong, or other 'what-if' scenarios?

I don't really have a lot of "what-if" scenarios running through my head, and I'm not exactly worried that I won't be able to handle it. It's really just the workload itself. It's the sheer amount of things they expect us to do for this rollout on top of my normal teaching duties. I just look at the list of everything that needs to get done, and that's what makes me feel so on edge. It's just the volume of the work, really.

Over these past five months, would you say you've been feeling that on-edge feeling on more days than not, or is it more like certain days or certain weeks when you're thinking about the school stuff?

I wouldn't say it's more days than not. It really just depends on what's going on at school. It's more like... certain days or weeks. 

If we have a big deadline coming up for the rollout, or if they just dumped a bunch of new paperwork on us, then I'll definitely feel it for a few days. But if it's a normal week and I can just focus on my students without all the extra district noise, I'm fine. So, yeah, it's really just tied to those specific times when the workload spikes.
Before the school district gave you this new rollout assignment five months ago, did you ever experience that on-edge feeling at all, even occasionally or in milder form?

No, not really. Before they added this bilingual SEL rollout to my plate, I was managing my usual teaching load and everything else just fine. It was really only within the first month or two of them dumping all this extra work on me that I started feeling this way... just really unlike myself. So, no, I didn't have that feeling before this all started five months ago.

You mentioned this started about five months ago. Has that on-edge feeling been present consistently throughout all of these five months, or did it start and then stop at some point before picking back up again?

It's been pretty consistent throughout the whole five months. I mean, like I said, it flares up more on certain days when the workload is heavier, but the general feeling... it hasn't really stopped since they assigned me this rollout role midyear. It's just been an ongoing thing for five months now.

You mentioned this started about five months ago when the district assigned you the rollout role. Just to be clear on the timeline—are you saying it's been exactly five months, or has it been longer than that?
No, it hasn't been longer than that. It's been right about five months... ever since the district assigned me that rollout role midyear. So, yeah, five months is the timeline.

You said this started about five months ago. Looking back, would you say it's been a full five months, or could it have actually started a bit earlier—maybe six months ago or longer—and you're just remembering it as starting around when the rollout was assigned?

No, I'm sure it hasn't been longer than that. It's really just been going on for about five months. I know for a fact it started right when the district assigned me that rollout role midyear. Before that, everything was fine.

You mentioned you're still getting your work done despite feeling on edge. But overall, would you say this on-edge feeling has significantly interfered with your ability to do your job, your relationships, or your daily life—or is it more just an uncomfortable feeling you're experiencing while still managing everything?

Well, I am still teaching and meeting my basic responsibilities in the classroom. It hasn't stopped me from doing my job entirely. But... it has definitely affected things. I've missed or had to push back some of my planning deadlines recently, which isn't like me. And I've actually needed reminders from my colleagues for a few tasks that I used to just complete reliably on my own. So I am managing, but I'm definitely not as on top of things as I normally am.

If the school district were to remove you from this rollout assignment tomorrow, do you think that on-edge feeling would go away fairly quickly, or do you think it might stick around for a while even without that work pressure?

I really think it would go away fairly quickly. The thing is, those rollout responsibilities are still ongoing right now. I'm still dealing with it every day. So... I haven't had a chance to see if these feelings would stick around after the situation ends, just because it hasn't ended yet. But if they took it off my plate tomorrow? Yes, I think that on-edge feeling would fade pretty fast.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a clear situational anxiety disorder (Generalized Anxiety Disorder, Unspecified) triggered by a specific psychosocial stressor (new work assignment). Key diagnostic features include: (1) persistent on-edge feeling for 5 months, (2) direct temporal relationship to identifiable stressor (district rollout assignment), (3) symptoms largely confined to work-related contexts and absent in other situations, (4) mild functional impairment (procrastination on lesson plans, avoidance of emails, reliance on colleague reminders), (5) absence of depressed mood, racing thoughts, or significant physical symptoms, and (6) expected resolution if stressor is removed. The 5-month duration meets the minimum threshold for anxiety disorder diagnosis. F06.8 (Other specified mental disorder due to known physiological condition) was considered but is less appropriate as no medical condition is identified as the primary etiology.
